header:
Date: 2025-05-14
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Anna Lee (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (CTO - SapinTech), Daniel Ortiz (Sr ML Eng), Liam Harper (DevOps)
Recording: yes
Notes: Integration-focused discovery; customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; heavy interest in LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, gateway/proxy pattern, rate limiting, and observability hooks
transcript:
[00:00] Anna: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Anna from Redwood, AE on this account, and Marcus will dive into integration details. How's everyone's afternoon?
[00:06] Priya: Good, thanks. Busy day. We'll try to be concise.
[00:10] Marcus: Great. Quick agenda — SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, how you'd run via a gateway or proxy, rate limits/quotas, and observability hooks. We'll leave time for Q&A.
[00:18] Daniel: Perfect. For context, we have a prod app that uses LangChain heavily, some homegrown connectors, and we're exploring migrating model calls off of in-house GPUs to either hosted Redwood or dedicated for stable latency. Security is a must — SSO and VPC stuff.
[00:34] Anna: Noted. Priya, can you share the primary integration constraints — latency SLOs, throughput, whether you need on-prem?
[00:40] Priya: Latency targets are 150-300ms P95 for short responses, but for multi-turn chat it's softer. Throughput is bursty — 200 rps sustained during peak, but we have spiky peaks to 700 rps for short windows. Data residency: US and EU.
[00:55] Marcus: Okay — that makes sense. On the SDK side, Redwood has official SDKs in Python, Node, and Go; they support streaming, function/tool calling, and we have a LangChain adapter and examples for LlamaIndex. The adapter maps Redwood's streaming tokens into LangChain StreamHandler — it's been used in a few customers.
[01:12] Daniel: Is the adapter maintained by Redwood or community? Any breaking changes?
[01:16] Marcus: Redwood maintains an official adapter repo, we tag releases aligned with runtime changes. We try to keep semver and document breaking changes in the changelog. For customers needing a pinned behavior we recommend pinning SDK + model version.
[01:26] Liam: For private deployments, do those adapters change? Our security team wants minimal inbound connections and prefers egress through our gateway.
[01:32] Marcus: Good Q. The adapter itself is library-level; for private deployments the SDK points at your private control plane endpoint. If you run Redwood Private behind a proxy/gateway, the SDK supports custom base URLs and TLS cert validation. You can also run an internal sidecar/proxy that does auth and rate-limiting.
[01:51] Priya: We were picturing a gateway pattern — one internal API that fans out to Redwood or fallback local models. Does Redwood support automatic fallback between hosted and dedicated/private?
[02:00] Anna: Yes, the routing layer can be policy-driven. For example, you'd route by availability or cost — primary to Dedicated, fallback to Hosted, etc. Marcus can run through how we'd configure that.
[02:09] Marcus: Absolutely. We expose routing policies in the control plane — region, model variant, and cost tiers. For a gateway, it's common to have a single internal endpoint that enforces auth and quotas, then proxies to Redwood with per-tenant API keys. If you want, our SDK supports token rotation hooks so the gateway can exchange short-lived tokens.
[02:28] Daniel: About quotas — we plan to enforce per-customer quotas and heavier rate limiting during peaks. Can Redwood do per-api-key quotas and burst windows?
[02:36] Marcus: Yes — per-key throttling and quota buckets. We also have burst tokens you can configure on Dedicated to handle short spikes. On Hosted, quotas are enforced at the account and route level; Dedicated gives you finer isolation and dedicated GPU pools, which helps with predictable throughput.
[02:51] Priya: And metric/observability — we need traces, token-level cost breakdowns, latency per route, and the ability to hook into our existing observability stack (Datadog + OpenTelemetry).
[03:02] Marcus: We emit detailed metrics and traces. There are two main hooks: 1) server-side metrics you can pull via the Console and APIs, and 2) SDK client-side hooks — you can register callbacks for request start/end, streaming token events, and errors. For traces we support OpenTelemetry spans and correlate trace IDs.
[03:20] Daniel: Any gotchas on correlating logs from our gateway proxy and Redwood traces?
[03:24] Marcus: Best practice is to propagate a trace-id header from your gateway to Redwood; our SDK will attach it to spans. If you terminate TLS at a proxy, ensure the X-Forwarded-For and trace headers are preserved.
[03:36] Liam: For our network architecture, we'd prefer to minimize outgoing connections; ideally the gateway keeps a small pool to Redwood endpoints. Does the SDK support connection pooling and HTTP/2 or gRPC?
[03:45] Marcus: SDKs use HTTP/2 where available and keep persistent connections. For higher throughput we recommend using our streaming endpoints which leverage long-lived connections to reduce TLS handshakes. For internal gateways, keep a fixed-size pool to Redwood endpoints; that pattern performs well.
[04:00] Priya: About LlamaIndex — we rely on LlamaIndex for retrieval-augmented generation. Does Redwood have any specific integrations to avoid re-tokenizing or to support prefix caching?
[04:09] Marcus: We have prefix and KV cache features in the runtime. For RAG, you can use the SDK to push embeddings and cache common prefixes or skeleton prompts. Our LlamaIndex example demonstrates native prompt templates and how to re-use KV cache across similar sessions to reduce tokens. The example isn't magic — you'll need to adapt retrieval sizes, but it's a solid starting point.
[04:31] Daniel: Token accounting — we need per-request token breakdown so we can allocate costs to features. Is that exposed?
[04:36] Marcus: Yes — Console and the usage APIs give token breakdowns per request, with model tokens, prompt tokens, and streaming tokens broken out. We also provide SDK call metadata so you can log cost attribution in your own system.
[04:47] Priya: On the security side, we require SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and audit logs for admin actions. Are these available across hosted/dedicated/private?
[04:58] Anna: SAML + SCIM and audit logs are available on Dedicated and Private. Hosted supports SSO and audit trails but certain SCIM automation and extended log retention is an enterprise add-on. We'll share the security matrix.
[05:12] Liam: If we do Private on-prem, what are the options for KMS? We use AWS KMS and a hardware HSM for keys.
[05:18] Marcus: Private supports KMS integrations, including AWS KMS and customer-managed HSMs. On-prem deployments can be configured to use your KMS and keys never leave the customer's boundary. We'll include the deployment doc link in the notes.
[05:31] Daniel: For testing, we want to run a bench that mirrors our spiky traffic. Can Redwood run a bench against a Dedicated pool and then fail over to Hosted to observe latency/throughput differences?
[05:40] Marcus: Yes — we can spin up an ephemeral Dedicated pool with a pinned model, run a benchmark, and configure automated fallback to Hosted. For the bench we'll want your workload traces or a generated load profile that matches your 700 rps spikes.
[05:52] Priya: About observability hooks again — can streaming token events be forwarded to our Kafka cluster or does it only go to Datadog/OTel?
[06:00] Marcus: We have webhooks and direct OTel exporters. For streaming token events, the common approach is to use the SDK streaming callbacks to forward to your pipeline (e.g., Kafka). If you prefer server-side fan-out, we can enable server-webhooks for completed responses. There is a small tradeoff on per-token forwarding for high throughput due to volume — usually customers batch events client-side.
[06:22] Daniel: Got it. Any limitations with LangChain or LlamaIndex — e.g., function-calling, streaming, or tool invocation?
[06:28] Marcus: Function-calling is fully supported — we map Redwood function-tool schema to LangChain tool interface in the adapter. Streaming tools work but you'd handle partial outputs in your stream handler. Occasionally transcription of tool names or model names is off in logs — small nuisance.
[06:42] Priya: For our compliance team, can we get a retention policy that deletes prompt content after X days on Hosted?
[06:49] Anna: Hosted has configurable retention windows, but Dedicated and Private give you more control. We'll include the exact retention SLAs in the security doc.
[06:59] Liam: On rate limits — what's the behavior when a client hits the quota? 429s only, or queueing/backoff options?
[07:06] Marcus: By default we return 429s; but for Dedicated you can enable token bucket bursting and queuing at the routing layer. For gateways it's often simpler to return a polite 429 and implement client-side exponential backoff.
[07:17] Daniel: Any SDK-specific gotchas for retries to avoid duplicate charges or duplicate side-effects?
[07:22] Marcus: Yes — the SDK exposes idempotency keys for generation requests and recommends retries only for network/timeouts while preserving idempotency. For streaming responses retries can be trickier — better to design idempotent downstream effects.
[07:34] Priya: We'll need a demo of the LangChain adapter plugged into one of our notebook workflows — something Marcus can run with our sample RAG index?
[07:41] Anna: That's a clear next step — Marcus, can you assemble a short notebook + repo and runbook?
[07:45] Marcus: Yep — I'll prepare a repo with LangChain and LlamaIndex examples, plus a notebook that uses a small sample dataset. I'll include instructions for using the SDK with a proxy and trace propagation.
[07:56] Priya: About observability again — we have a requirement to produce cost reports per product line monthly. Can Redwood's billing exports be broken down to our internal product tags?
[08:05] Marcus: We support tagging at the request level. If you send a product tag header, it gets associated with usage and exported in billing CSVs.
[08:12] Liam: For Private deployments, what about upgrades — downtime windows?
[08:16] Marcus: Private has rolling upgrades pattern; typical maintenance windows are configurable. For Dedicated, we aim for zero-downtime scheduling using live model swapping. We'll provide the upgrade SLA doc.
[08:27] Daniel: Any suggestion on quantization/ model variants for cost savings — e.g., 8-bit quantized runners?
[08:33] Marcus: We support quantized model variants and the runtime chooses kernels accordingly. For many RAG use-cases a 4-bit/8-bit quantized candidate model for reranking and a full precision for final generation works well. Redwood Optimize can recommend profiles based on your workload.
[08:47] Priya: Ok let's wrap with a quick recap and owners.
[08:50] Anna: Recap — Marcus will send LangChain/LlamaIndex example repo and an SDK streaming example, Anna will send pricing/security docs, Liam will provide network details, and SapinTech will decide pilot scope and dataset.
[09:03] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:06] Anna: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench and pilot kickoff.
[09:10] End of recording.
